# Conceptual foundations

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## What fitting means

Choose the parameters $\theta = (\beta, \gamma)$ so that the model's output is [as close as possible]{style="color: tomato;"} to the data $\mathbf{y}$

- The whole question is what *close* means
- Whatever we decide, we write it as a number: an [objective function]{style="color: tomato;"} $\mathcal{L}(\theta, \mathbf{y})$ that is small when the curve is near the data and large when it is far away
- Fitting is then a search over $\theta$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Two ways to answer

### A point estimate

$$\hat{\theta} = \arg\min_{\theta} \mathcal{L}(\theta, \mathbf{y})$$

The next two sections are two choices of $\mathcal{L}$: the sum of squared errors, then the negative log-likelihood

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### A distribution

Instead of the one best $\theta$, a probability for *every* $\theta$ given the data

$$p(\theta \mid \mathbf{y})$$

That is Bayesian inference, and it is where the lecture ends up. The likelihood we build in section 4 is the bridge between the two answers

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Why the model will never match the data exactly {.smaller}

Even with the right $\beta$ and $\gamma$ the curve will not pass through every point. The mismatch has several sources, and each is handled somewhere in this lecture

| Source | In the flu data | Where we deal with it |
|---|---|---|
| Observation | Not every pupil in bed was infectious, or counted | The likelihood (4) |
| Parameter | Several $(\beta, \gamma)$ pairs fit almost as well | Confidence intervals (4), the posterior (6) |
| Model | No latent period; everyone mixes with everyone | Model comparison (4) |
| Process | Chance in who infected whom, day by day | Particle filtering (7) |

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Identifiability {.smaller}

[**The problem:**]{style="color: tomato;"} different parameter combinations can produce nearly the same curve

- A high $\beta$ with a high $\gamma$: fast spread, quick recovery
- A low $\beta$ with a low $\gamma$: slow spread, long infections
- Both can give a similar epidemic, because the data mostly pin down $R_0 = \beta N / \gamma$, not $\beta$ and $\gamma$ separately

You will see this as a tilted valley in the least squares surface, as wide profile likelihoods, and as a tilted cloud of posterior samples

[**The way out:**]{style="color: tomato;"} bring in what you already know, such as a plausible infectious period for influenza. In the Bayesian section that is exactly what a prior is

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Where to start

The simplest possible objective function: the sum of squared distances between the points and the curve
